claim: TAK1 is a serine/threonine protein kinase that is a key regulator in a wide variety of cellular processes.
source: TAK1 is a serine/threonine protein kinase that is a key regulator in a wide variety of cellular processes.
evidence: This is a general statement about TAK1 that draws from established scientific knowledge about this kinase.

claim: TAK1 knockdown promoted esophageal squamous cancer carcinoma (ESCC) migration and invasion.
source: Here, we found that TAK1 knockdown promoted esophageal squamous cancer carcinoma (ESCC) migration and invasion, whereas TAK1 overexpression resulted in the opposite outcome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro studies shown in the manuscript.

claim: TAK1 overexpression resulted in the opposite outcome to TAK1 knockdown on ESCC migration and invasion.
source: Here, we found that TAK1 knockdown promoted esophageal squamous cancer carcinoma (ESCC) migration and invasion, whereas TAK1 overexpression resulted in the opposite outcome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro studies shown in the manuscript.

claim: In vitro findings on TAK1's effects on ESCC migration and invasion were recapitulated in vivo in a xenograft metastatic mouse model.
source: These in vitro findings were recapitulated in vivo in a xenograft metastatic mouse model.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TAK1 interacted with phospholipase C epsilon 1 (PLCE1).
source: Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry demonstrated that TAK1 interacted with phospholipase C epsilon 1 (PLCE1) and phosphorylated PLCE1 at serine 1060 (S1060).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data.

claim: TAK1 phosphorylated PLCE1 at serine 1060 (S1060).
source: Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry demonstrated that TAK1 interacted with phospholipase C epsilon 1 (PLCE1) and phosphorylated PLCE1 at serine 1060 (S1060).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data.

claim: Phosphorylation at S1060 in PLCE1 resulted in decreased enzyme activity.
source: Functional studies revealed that phosphorylation at S1060 in PLCE1 resulted in decreased enzyme activity, leading to the repression of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) hydrolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enzyme activity assay data.

claim: Phosphorylation at S1060 in PLCE1 led to the repression of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) hydrolysis.
source: Functional studies revealed that phosphorylation at S1060 in PLCE1 resulted in decreased enzyme activity, leading to the repression of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) hydrolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enzyme activity assay data.

claim: The degradation products of PIP2 including diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol IP3 were reduced by TAK1-mediated phosphorylation of PLCE1.
source: As a result, the degradation products of PIP2 including diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol IP3 were reduced, which thereby suppressed signal transduction in the axis of PKC/GSK-3β/β-Catenin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of IP3 and DAG levels.

claim: Reduction of PIP2 degradation products suppressed signal transduction in the axis of PKC/GSK-3β/β-Catenin.
source: As a result, the degradation products of PIP2 including diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol IP3 were reduced, which thereby suppressed signal transduction in the axis of PKC/GSK-3β/β-Catenin.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing changes in PKC, GSK-3β, and β-Catenin phosphorylation.

claim: Expression of cancer metastasis-related genes was impeded by TAK1.
source: Consequently, expression of cancer metastasis-related genes was impeded by TAK1.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data showing changes in EMT-related gene expression.

claim: TAK1 plays a negative role in ESCC metastasis.
source: Overall, our data indicate that TAK1 plays a negative role in ESCC metastasis, which depends on the TAK1-induced phosphorylation of PLCE1 at S1060.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data including in vitro and in vivo studies.

claim: TAK1's negative role in ESCC metastasis depends on the TAK1-induced phosphorylation of PLCE1 at S1060.
source: Overall, our data indicate that TAK1 plays a negative role in ESCC metastasis, which depends on the TAK1-induced phosphorylation of PLCE1 at S1060.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional studies using PLCE1 S1060A mutant.

claim: Esophageal cancer (EC) is the seventh most common malignancy worldwide, with more than 600,000 new cases diagnosed annually.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The primary histological subtypes of EC include esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and esophageal adenocarcinoma.
source: The primary histological subtypes of EC include esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and esophageal adenocarcinoma (He et al., 2021; Lagergren et al., 2017).

claim: ESCC is a major subtype of EC in China, accounting for more than 90% of EC.

claim: The early diagnosis rate of ESCC is very low owing to the lack of specific biomarkers.
source: The early diagnosis rate of ESCC is very low owing to the lack of specific biomarkers.

claim: Most ESCC patients are found to be in locally advanced or metastatic stages when they are diagnosed.

claim: The 5-year survival rate of ESCC is approximately 15–25%.

claim: Recurrence and metastasis remain significant challenges in ESCC treatment.

claim: TAK1 is encoded by the gene Map3k7.

evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about TAK1.

claim: TAK1 has been shown to play an integral role in inflammatory signal transduction through multiple pathways.

claim: TAK1 is involved in a wide variety of cellular processes, including cell survival, cell migration and invasion, inflammation, immune regulation, and tumorigenesis.
source: TAK1 is involved in a wide variety of cellular processes, including cell survival, cell migration and invasion, inflammation, immune regulation, and tumorigenesis (Cho et al., 2021; Mukhopadhyay and Lee, 2020).

claim: TAK1 has been shown to negatively associated with tumor progression in several human cancers including prostate cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cervical cancer, and certain blood cancers.
source: For example, by acting as a tumor suppressor, TAK1 has been shown to negatively associated with tumor progression in several human cancers including prostate cancer (Huang et al., 2021), hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (Tan et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021), cervical cancer (Guan et al., 2017), and certain blood cancers (Guo et al., 2019).

claim: TAK1 promotes tumor progression in a variety of human cancers, including colon, ovarian, lung, and breast cancers.

claim: TAK1 plays a dual role in tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis.
source: These aforementioned findings indicate that TAK1 plays a dual role in tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis.

claim: TAK1 has been shown to phosphorylate RASSF9 at serine 284 to inhibit cell proliferation by targeting the RAS/MEK/ERK axis in ESCC.
source: In our previous study, TAK1 has been shown to phosphorylate RASSF9 at serine 284 to inhibit cell proliferation by targeting the RAS/MEK/ERK axis in ESCC (Shi et al., 2021).

claim: To date, there have been no reports on the precise role of TAK1 in ESCC metastasis.
source: To date, there have been no reports on the precise role of TAK1 in ESCC metastasis.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Phospholipase C epsilon 1 (PLCE1) is encoded by the Plce1 gene on chromosome 10q23 in human.
source: Phospholipase C epsilon 1 (PLCE1) is encoded by the Plce1 gene on chromosome 10q23 in human and belongs to the phospholipase C (PLC) family (Fukami et al., 2010; Kadamur and Ross, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PLCE1 belongs to the phospholipase C (PLC) family.
source: Phospholipase C epsilon 1 (PLCE1) is encoded by the Plce1 gene on chromosome 10q23 in human and belongs to the phospholipase C (PLC) family (Fukami et al., 2010; Kadamur and Ross, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PLCE1 is composed of a PLC catalytic domain, PH domain, EF domain, and C2 domain.
source: Like other PLC family members, PLCE1 is composed of a PLC catalytic domain, PH domain, EF domain, and C2 domain.
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about PLCE1 structure.

claim: PLCE1 contains unique regions, two C-terminal Ras association (RA) domains and an N-terminal CDC25-homology domain.
source: In addition, PLCE1 contains unique regions, two C-terminal Ras association (RA) domains and an N-terminal CDC25-homology domain (Kadamur and Ross, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Once activated, PLCE1 is essential for intracellular signaling by catalyzing the hydrolysis of membrane phospholipids such as phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
source: Once activated, PLCE1 is essential for intracellular signaling by catalyzing the hydrolysis of membrane phospholipids such as phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), in order to produce two important secondary messengers, inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG), which further trigger IP3-dependent calcium ion (Ca2+) release from the endoplasmic reticulum and PKC activation (Fukami et al., 2010; Kadamur and Ross, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PLCE1 catalyzes the hydrolysis of PIP2 to produce two important secondary messengers, inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG).
source: Once activated, PLCE1 is essential for intracellular signaling by catalyzing the hydrolysis of membrane phospholipids such as phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), in order to produce two important secondary messengers, inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG), which further trigger IP3-dependent calcium ion (Ca2+) release from the endoplasmic reticulum and PKC activation (Fukami et al., 2010; Kadamur and Ross, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IP3 and DAG trigger IP3-dependent calcium ion (Ca2+) release from the endoplasmic reticulum and PKC activation.
source: Once activated, PLCE1 is essential for intracellular signaling by catalyzing the hydrolysis of membrane phospholipids such as phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), in order to produce two important secondary messengers, inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG), which further trigger IP3-dependent calcium ion (Ca2+) release from the endoplasmic reticulum and PKC activation (Fukami et al., 2010; Kadamur and Ross, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PLCE1 promotes cell growth, migration, and metastasis in multiple human cancers, including hepatocellular carcinoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, head and neck cancer, bladder cancer, gastric cancer, and prostate cancer.
source: Accumulating evidence has shown that PLCE1 promotes cell growth, migration, and metastasis in multiple human cancers, including hepatocellular carcinoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, head and neck cancer, bladder cancer, gastric cancer, and prostate cancer (Abnet et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2019; Liao et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2011; Ou et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Whether and how PLCE1 affects cancer metastasis in ESCC remain largely unknown.
source: However, whether and how PLCE1 affects cancer metastasis in ESCC remain largely unknown.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: TAK1 expression was reduced in esophageal squamous tumor tissues.
source: In our previous study, we showed that TAK1 expression was reduced in esophageal squamous tumor tissues, and that TAK1 inhibits ESCC proliferation (Shi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: TAK1 inhibits ESCC proliferation.
source: In our previous study, we showed that TAK1 expression was reduced in esophageal squamous tumor tissues, and that TAK1 inhibits ESCC proliferation (Shi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: EGF treatment induced a spindle-shaped morphology in ECA-109 cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, EGF treatment induced a spindle-shaped morphology in ECA-109 cells, which was markedly prevented by TAK1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TAK1 markedly prevented EGF-induced spindle-shaped morphology in ECA-109 cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, EGF treatment induced a spindle-shaped morphology in ECA-109 cells, which was markedly prevented by TAK1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TAK1 is a negative regulator of EMT in ESCC.
source: These data implied that TAK1 is a negative regulator of EMT in ESCC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing TAK1's effects on EMT-related morphology and gene expression.

claim: TAK1 repressed the migration and invasion of ECA-109 cells.
source: To address this hypothesis, we performed a transwell assay and found that TAK1 repressed the migration and invasion of ECA-109 cells (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TAK1 increased E-cadherin and ZO-1, two epithelial molecules.
source: Our data showed that TAK1 increased E-cadherin and ZO-1, two epithelial molecules, whereas mesenchymal molecules such as N-cadherin, Vimentin, and ZEB1 were reduced by TAK1 (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mesenchymal molecules such as N-cadherin, Vimentin, and ZEB1 were reduced by TAK1.
source: Our data showed that TAK1 increased E-cadherin and ZO-1, two epithelial molecules, whereas mesenchymal molecules such as N-cadherin, Vimentin, and ZEB1 were reduced by TAK1 (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TAK1 knockdown induced F-Actin expression.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, TAK1 knockdown induced F-Actin expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: TAK1 knockdown promoted a spindle-shaped mesenchymal morphology in ECA-109 cells.
source: TAK1 knockdown promoted a spindle-shaped mesenchymal morphology in ECA-109 cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Cell invasion and migration were stimulated by TAK1 knockdown.
source: In accordance with these changes, cell invasion and migration were stimulated, as evidenced by data from the wound healing and transwell assays (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by wound healing and transwell assay data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The epithelial markers including E-cadherin and Claudin-1 were found to have decreased by TAK1 knockdown.
source: The epithelial markers including E-cadherin and Claudin-1 were found to have decreased by TAK1 knockdown, whereas mesenchymal markers N-cadherin, Vimentin, Snail, and Slug were increased (Figure 1I; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Mesenchymal markers N-cadherin, Vimentin, Snail, and Slug were increased by TAK1 knockdown.
source: The epithelial markers including E-cadherin and Claudin-1 were found to have decreased by TAK1 knockdown, whereas mesenchymal markers N-cadherin, Vimentin, Snail, and Slug were increased (Figure 1I; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: TAK1 negatively regulates ESCC migration and invasion.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that TAK1 negatively regulates ESCC migration and invasion.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data from gain-of-function and loss-of-function studies.

claim: The serine residue at position 1060 (S1060) in PLCE1 was phosphorylated.
source: According to the mass spectrometry data, the serine residue at position 1060 (S1060) in PLCE1 was phosphorylated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Wildtype (WT) PLCE1 was phosphorylated by TAK1 at S1060.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, wildtype (WT) PLCE1 was phosphorylated by TAK1 at S1060, whereas PCLE1 S1060A was resistant to TAK1-induced phosphorylation at S1060.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PCLE1 S1060A was resistant to TAK1-induced phosphorylation at S1060.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, wildtype (WT) PLCE1 was phosphorylated by TAK1 at S1060, whereas PCLE1 S1060A was resistant to TAK1-induced phosphorylation at S1060.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The p-PLCE1 S1060 induced by TAK1 was weakened by (5Z)-7-oxozeaenol (Oxo).
source: Moreover, the p-PLCE1 S1060 induced by TAK1 was weakened by(5Z)-7-oxozeaenol (Oxo), a potent inhibitor of TAK1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Phosphorylated TAK1 (p-TAK1) markedly decreased in the presence of Oxo.
source: Notably, phosphorylated TAK1 (p-TAK1) markedly decreased in the presence of Oxo, indicating that TAK1 was inhibited (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TAK1 was inhibited by Oxo.
source: Notably, phosphorylated TAK1 (p-TAK1) markedly decreased in the presence of Oxo, indicating that TAK1 was inhibited (Figure 2C).

claim: PLCE1 was phosphorylated by TAK1 at serine 1060 in an in vitro kinase assay.
source: Moreover, the in vitro kinase assay showed that PLCE1 was phosphorylated by TAK1 at serine 1060 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PLCE1 is a downstream target of TAK1.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that PLCE1 is a downstream target of TAK1, and that PLCE1 S1060 is phosphorylated by TAK1.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data including co-immunoprecipitation, mass spectrometry, and kinase assays.

claim: PLCE1 S1060 is phosphorylated by TAK1.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that PLCE1 is a downstream target of TAK1, and that PLCE1 S1060 is phosphorylated by TAK1.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data including co-immunoprecipitation, mass spectrometry, and kinase assays.

claim: TAK1 expression was reduced in tumor tissues compared to that in their respective adjacent normal tissues.
source: As shown in Figure 2F, TAK1 expression was reduced in tumor tissues compared to that in their respective adjacent normal tissues.

claim: p-PLCE1 levels were decreased in tumor tissues.
source: In accordance with these changes in TAK1, p-PLCE1 levels were also decreased in tumor tissues (Figure 2G)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: TAK1 expression was positively correlated with p-PLCE1 expression.
source: Pearson's correlation tests showed that TAK1 expression was positively correlated with p-PLCE1 expression (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Pearson's correlation analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: PLCE1 positively regulates ESCC migration and invasion.
source: Overall, these data clearly indicate that PLCE1 positively regulates ESCC migration and invasion.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data from gain-of-function and loss-of-function studies.

claim: By inducing phosphorylation at S1060, TAK1 inhibits PLCE1 enzyme activity.
source: By inducing phosphorylation at S1060, TAK1 inhibits PLCE1 enzyme activity, thereby counteracting PLCE1-induced ESCC migration and invasion.

claim: TAK1 counteracts PLCE1-induced ESCC migration and invasion.
source: By inducing phosphorylation at S1060, TAK1 inhibits PLCE1 enzyme activity, thereby counteracting PLCE1-induced ESCC migration and invasion.
evidence: This claim is supported by transwell and wound healing assay data.

claim: PLCE1 is a downstream target of TAK1 that inhibits ESCC migration and invasion.
source: PLCE1 is a downstream target of TAK1 that inhibits ESCC migration and invasion.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data showing the TAK1-PLCE1 interaction and functional consequences.

claim: PLCE1 overexpression significantly increased the migration and invasion in ECA-109 cells.
source: In ECA-109 cells, PLCE1 overexpression significantly increased the migration and invasion (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by transwell and wound healing assay data shown in Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The epithelial marker E-cadherin was repressed by PLCE1.
source: In accordance with these changes, the epithelial marker E-cadherin was repressed by PLCE1, whereas the mesenchymal markers including Vimentin, Snail, Slug, and ZEB-1 were activated (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The mesenchymal markers including Vimentin, Snail, Slug, and ZEB-1 were activated by PLCE1.
source: In accordance with these changes, the epithelial marker E-cadherin was repressed by PLCE1, whereas the mesenchymal markers including Vimentin, Snail, Slug, and ZEB-1 were activated (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PLCE1 knockdown impeded cell migration and invasion.

evidence: This claim is supported by transwell and wound healing assay data shown in Figure 3G and H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The PLCE1 activity was reduced in the presence of TAK1.

claim: The PLCE1 S1060A activity was not affected by TAK1.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, the PLCE1 activity was reduced in the presence of TAK1; however, the PLCE1 S1060A activity was not affected (Figure 4B), indicating TAK1-induced phosphorylation at S1060 repressed PLCE1 activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TAK1-induced phosphorylation at S1060 repressed PLCE1 activity.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, the PLCE1 activity was reduced in the presence of TAK1; however, the PLCE1 S1060A activity was not affected (Figure 4B), indicating TAK1-induced phosphorylation at S1060 repressed PLCE1 activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of TAK1 on wildtype PLCE1 versus PLCE1 S1060A.

claim: The productions of IP3 and DAG were increased by PLCE1.
source: Our data showed that the productions of IP3 and DAG were increased by PLCE1, which was largely counteracted by TAK1 (Figure 4C and E).

claim: PLCE1-induced IP3 and DAG production was largely counteracted by TAK1.
source: Our data showed that the productions of IP3 and DAG were increased by PLCE1, which was largely counteracted by TAK1 (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: IP3 induces the endoplasmic reticulum to release Ca2+ into the cytoplasm.
source: As a messenger, IP3 induces the endoplasmic reticulum to release Ca2+ into the cytoplasm (Kadamur and Ross, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The signals for the cytoplasmic Ca2+ were increased by PLCE1 in ECA-109 cells.

claim: PLCE1-induced cytoplasmic Ca2+ increase was attenuated by TAK1.
source: As expected, the signals for the cytoplasmic Ca2+ were increased by PLCE1 in ECA-109 cells, and this trend was attenuated by TAK1 (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Fluo-4 AM staining data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: TAK1 inhibits PLCE1 activity.

claim: TAK1 inhibition of PLCE1 activity is likely due to TAK1-induced phosphorylation of PLCE1 at S1060.
source: This evidence indicates that TAK1 inhibits PLCE1 activity, which is likely due to TAK1-induced phosphorylation of PLCE1 at S1060.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of TAK1 on wildtype PLCE1 versus PLCE1 S1060A.

claim: TAK1 reversed PLCE1-induced cell migration and invasion.

evidence: This claim is supported by transwell and wound healing assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAK1 failed to affect PLCE1 S1060A-induced cell migration and invasion.

evidence: This claim is supported by transwell and wound healing assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAK1 overexpression induced increases in p-IKK, p-JNK, p-p38 MAPK, and p-ERK in ECA-109 cells.

claim: TAK1 knockdown reduced p-IKK, p-JNK, p-p38 MAPK, and p-ERK protein levels.
source: For example, TAK1 overexpression induced increases in p-IKK, p-JNK, p-p38 MAPK, and p-ERK in ECA-109 cells, whereas TAK1 knockdown reduced these protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: PLCE1 is likely a unique substrate of TAK1 for transducing its inhibitory effects on ESCC migration and invasion.
source: At this regard, PLCE1 is likely a unique substrate of TAK1 for transducing its inhibitory effects on ESCC migration and invasion, although some other signaling pathways are also affected by TAK1.

claim: PKC is a promising downstream target of intracellular Ca2+.
source: PKC is a promising downstream target of intracellular Ca2+ (Kadamur and Ross, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: PKC positively regulates the expression and stability of β-Catenin in a GSK-3β-dependent manner.
source: It has been shown that PKC positively regulates the expression and stability of β-Catenin in a GSK-3β-dependent manner (Duong et al., 2017; Gwak et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2018; Ryu and Han, 2015; Tejeda-Muñoz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: β-Catenin is considered as a positive regulator in the EMT process.
source: Of note, β-Catenin is considered as a positive regulator in the EMT process (Valenta et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: PLCE1 stimulates cell migration and invasion via the axis of PKC/GSK-3β/β-Catenin.
source: Therefore, we predicted that PLCE1 stimulates cell migration and invasion via the axis of PKC/GSK-3β/β-Catenin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of IP3R, Ca2+, and PKC inhibitors on the PKC/GSK-3β/β-Catenin pathway.

claim: 2-APB treatment almost completely reversed PLCE1-induced the intracellular Ca2+.
source: In order to test this hypothesis, we treated cells with 2-APB, an IP3 receptor (IP3R) inhibitor, and found that 2-APB treatment almost completely reversed PLCE1-induced the intracellular Ca2+ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Fluo-4 AM staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PLCE1-induced cell migration and invasion were replenished by 2-APB in ECA-109 cells.
source: Accordingly, PLCE1-induced cell migration and invasion were replenished by 2-APB in ECA-109 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by transwell and wound healing assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Midostaurin almost completely abolished cell migration and invasion induced by PLCE1.
source: Therefore, we investigated whether the PLCE1-induced cell growth was dependent on PKC activation. To this end, midostaurin was used to inhibit PKC, and our data showed that midostaurin almost completely abolished cell migration and invasion induced by PLCE1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by transwell and wound healing assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: 2-APB, BAPTA-AM, and Midostaurin successfully inhibited PKC activity.
source: To test this prediction, ECA-109 cells were treated with an IP3R inhibitor (2-APB), Ca2+ chelator (BAPTA-AM), or PKC inhibitor (midostaurin), all of which successfully inhibited PKC activity, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylated PKC (p-PKC) (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 7A–C.

claim: Phosphorylated GSK-3b(p-GSK3b) was decreased by 2-APB, BAPTA-AM, and Midostaurin.
source: As a result, phosphorylated GSK-3b(p-GSK3b) was decreased by 2-APB, BAPTA-AM, and Midostaurin (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 7A–C), indicating GSK-3β kinase activity was upregulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 7A–C.

claim: GSK-3β kinase activity was upregulated by 2-APB, BAPTA-AM, and Midostaurin.
source: As a result, phosphorylated GSK-3b(p-GSK3b) was decreased by 2-APB, BAPTA-AM, and Midostaurin (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 7A–C), indicating GSK-3β kinase activity was upregulated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the decrease in p-GSK-3β levels.

claim: Phosphorylated β-Catenin (p-β-Catenin) was increased by 2-APB, BAPTA-AM, and Midostaurin.
source: Accordingly, phosphorylated β-Catenin (p-β-Catenin) was increased, leading to degradation of β-Catenin (Figure 5A-C; Figure 5—figure supplement 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 7A–C.

claim: Increased p-β-Catenin led to degradation of β-Catenin.
source: Accordingly, phosphorylated β-Catenin (p-β-Catenin) was increased, leading to degradation of β-Catenin (Figure 5A-C; Figure 5—figure supplement 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the increase in p-β-Catenin and decrease in total β-Catenin.

claim: MMP2 expression was inhibited by 2-APB, BAPTA-AM, and Midostaurin.
source: As a downstream target of β-Catenin, MMP2 expression was inhibited by all three tested chemicals (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 7A–C.

claim: PLCE1-induced β-Catenin expression could be counteracted by 2-APB, BAPTA-AM, and Midostaurin.
source: The immunofluorescence data also showed that PLCE1-induced β-Catenin expression could be counteracted by 2-APB, BAPTA-AM, and Midostaurin (Figure 5D).

claim: PLCE1-induced cell migration and invasion in ESCC are likely via the axis of PKC/GSK-3β/β-Catenin.
source: These results clearly indicate that PLCE1-induced cell migration and invasion in ESCC are likely via the axis of PKC/GSK-3β/β-Catenin.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data using inhibitors of IP3R, Ca2+, and PKC.
